case_name: Gold River Chinook Project Society v. Bowater Pulp and Paper Canada Inc.
text:
Citation:

Gold River Chinook Project Society v. Bowater Pulp
and Paper Canada Inc.

Date: 20020131

2002 BCSC 166

Docket:

S013364

Registry: Vancouver

IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

GOLD RIVER CHINOOK PROJECT SOCIETY

PLAINTIFF

AND:

BOWATER PULP AND PAPER CANADA INC.

DEFENDANT

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

OF THE

HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE BARROW

Counsel
for the Plaintiff:

William L. Roberts

Counsel
for the Defendant:

James H. Goulden

R. David House

Date
and Place of Hearing:

January 16, 2002

Vancouver, BC

[
1
] The defendant,
Bowater Pulp and Paper Canada Inc., applies for an order for security for costs
pursuant
s. 205
of the
Company Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 62, and the
inherent jurisdiction of this court.

[
2
] In order to
appreciate the relative merits of the parties' positions, some comment on the
background to this dispute is necessary.

[
3
] Until 1998, the
defendant (or its predecessors) operated a pulpmill on lands it owned in Gold
River, British Columbia. In August 1998, the defendant's pulpmill ceased
operations and in February 1999, the defendant formally closed the mill. The
lands upon which the mill is situate are presently for sale.

[
4
] The plaintiff,
Gold River Chinook Project Society, is a society incorporated under the laws of
the Province of British Columbia. Two of its five directors are Dale Frame and
his brother, John Frame. They are also the president and vice-president,
respectively, of the society. The plaintiff (or its predecessor) has operated a
salmon enhancement facility on the defendant's lands, adjacent to the
defendant's pulpmill, since 1983.

[
5
] The plaintiff
was incorporated to support and enhance the declining stocks of wild Chinook
and coho salmon in the rivers in the vicinity of Gold River. To accomplish
this, the plaintiff harvests wild salmon eggs from the area's rivers,
fertilizes and incubates them at its facilities, and raises them as fry until
they are mature enough to be returned to the streams from which they were
initially harvested. Over the past several years, the plaintiff has reared and
released approximately one million pacific salmon each year.

[
6
] Initially, the
plaintiff's operations consisted of garden shed and a stainless steel trough
that had been salvaged and refurbished from the defendant's mill. Over the 18
years of its existence, the plaintiff's operations grew to the point where, by
1999, they included two 150-foot by 45-foot rearing pools with associated
plumbing, a hatchery building, two ground water wells each 55 feet deep, a
30-foot galvanized above ground pool, pumps, well houses, and other related
equipment. Initially, the plaintiff's operations were carried out entirely by
volunteers. As of 1999, the plaintiff had three employees, one full-time and
two part-time. The full-time employee is the hatchery manager, Betty Frame, the
spouse of Dale Frame.

[
7
] Over the course
of its history, the plaintiff has received money or money's worth from various
sources in order to carry out its operations. The lands upon which its
operations are located belong to the defendant and have been made available to
the plaintiff without cost. Further, the defendant has provided telephone,
water, steam, power, oxygen, and maintenance services to the plaintiff, again
at no cost. The value of the power alone is approximately $2,700 per month.

[
8
] There are two
primary sources of revenue for the plaintiff: one is the Department of
Fisheries and Oceans, with whom the plaintiff contracts to raise and release
salmon, and the other is private aquaculture companies, with whom the plaintiff
contracts to raise Atlantic salmon for resale. One of the primary aquaculture
companies, with whom the plaintiff contracts, is Chin-Ho Aqua Ltd. Brian and
Dale Frame are both directors and officers of Chin-Ho Aqua.

[
9
] Adjacent to the
plaintiff's operations is an Atlantic salmon hatchery operated by Gold River
Smolt Company Ltd. The plaintiff's activities are carried out under a licence
issued by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. In August 2000, the plaintiff
and Gold River Smolt entered into a contract whereby Gold River Smolt agreed to
pay one-half of the plaintiff's licence cost (that is $3,000 per month). Gold
River Smolt further agreed to pay the plaintiff $3,000 per month unless and
until Gold River Smolt was granted a lease on the premises it was occupying.

[
10
] The defendant
was aware of and actively supported the plaintiff's activities. It made
reference to the plaintiff's activities in a variety of promotional materials
it issued in connection with the operation of its pulpmill.

[
11
] Over the
years, the plaintiff and the defendant discussed and exchanged correspondence
about the plaintiff's activities on the defendant's lands. No written contract,
however, was ever entered into between the parties in which their respective
interests were defined.

[
12
] As the
defendant began shutting its mill and prepared to sell the lands on which the
plaintiff's activities were being carried out, communications between the
parties as to the plaintiff's entitlement to occupy the land became more
frequent and more focussed. In spite of this, no agreement was reached and on
April 28, 2001, the defendant wrote to the plaintiff demanding that the latter
vacate the lands by May 31, 2001. The plaintiff had, in the spring of 2001,
substantial numbers of fish at various stages of maturity in its facilities.
After receiving the notice to vacate, the plaintiff commenced the within
action. In June 2001, the plaintiff applied for and was granted an interim
injunction, allowing it to remain on the property and continue its operations
for one year.

[
13
] In its
statement of claim, the primary relief sought by the plaintiff is a declaration
that it has an irrevocable licence to use and occupy the land on which its
operations are carried out. The defendant has filed a statement of defence and
a counter-claim. The primary relief sought in the counter-claim is a
declaration that the defendant is the owner in fee simple of the lands in issue
or, in the alternative, a declaration that the plaintiff has no right, title,
or interest in the lands.

ISSUES AND
THE POSITIONS OF THE PARTIES

[
14
]
Section 205
of
the
Company Act
provides as follows:

If
a corporation is plaintiff in an action or other legal proceeding and it
appears that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant
if the defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require security
to be given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all proceedings
until the security is given.

[
15
] In
Kropp
v. Swanest Bay Golf Course Ltd.
,
[1977] B.C.J. No. 593 (B.C.C.A.)
,
Finch J.A. (as he was then), at paragraph 17, distilled the following
principles from a review of various authorities, including specifically
Keary
Development v. Tarmac Construction
,
[1995] 3 All E.R. 534
:

1. The court has a
complete discretion whether to order security, and will act in light of all the
relevant circumstances;

2. The possibility
or probability that the plaintiff company will be deterred from pursuing its
claim is not without more sufficient reason for not ordering security;

3. The court must
attempt to balance injustices arising from use of security as an instrument of
oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of
impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the
other;

4. The court may
have regard to the merits of the action, but should avoid going into detail on
the merits unless success or failure appears obvious;

5. The court can
order any amount of security up to the full amount claimed, as long as the
amount is more than nominal;

6. Before the court
refuses to order security on the ground that it would unfairly stifle a valid
claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it is
probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7. The lateness of
the application for security is a circumstance which can properly be taken into
account.

[
16
] There are a
number of preconditions which must be satisfied before the discretion to make
an order for security for costs is engaged. Firstly, it is the obligation of
the applicant to demonstrate that, at least on a
prima facie
basis, the
plaintiff would be unable to pay the defendant's costs in the event the
plaintiff's action were to fail. If the applicant has satisfied the first
hurdle, it is open to the plaintiff to avoid an order for security for costs
being made against it by showing that it has sufficient exigible assets to
satisfy any potential award of costs. Further, the plaintiff may avoid such an
order if it can show that there is no arguable defence to its claim. I will
deal with these preliminary issues first and then turn to a consideration of
the matters which, in the circumstances of this case, are of importance in
determining how the courts discretion ought to be exercised.

[
17
] Before
addressing these issues, it is worth noting that the defendant has prepared a
draft bill of costs on the basis of which they are seeking security in the
amount of $45,600. The plaintiff, although resisting the application on various
bases, concedes that the amount claimed is otherwise reasonable.

ABILITY TO
PAY, EXIGIBLE ASSETS, ARGUABLE DEFENCE

[
18
] There is no
issue that, at least
prima facie
, the plaintiff does not have the
ability to pay the potential costs of the defendant if its action fails. The
material before me establishes and the plaintiff, in effect, concedes that all
of its revenue is consumed in its day-to-day operations.

[
19
] The plaintiff
does argue, however, that it has sufficient exigible assets to satisfy any
potential award of costs. In Mr. Frame's third affidavit, he deposes that the
plaintiff has a variety of movable assets consisting principally of motors, a
transformer, receiving pools, and the like, which have a resale value, in his
opinion, of approximately $119,000. In addition, he asserts that the plaintiff
has a variety of fixed assets consisting of buildings, concrete channels, and
underground piping. He estimates that these assets have a replacement cost of
$291,000. Finally, he says that there are other assets owned by the plaintiff
with an estimated resale value of $30,000.

[
20
] Mr. Frame was
cross-examined on his affidavit and in the process he acknowledged that he had
no real expertise or experience in selling used equipment. He frankly conceded
that his estimates relating to the movable assets are not resale values as his
affidavit states but rather replacement values. With respect to the fixed
assets, Mr. Frame states in his affidavit that his estimates are based on
replacement costs. Further, he stated in his cross-examination that several of
the fixed items have no resale value unless someone purchased the property on which
they are installed because, in order to move them, they would have to be
destroyed.

[
21
] The defendant
has employed a consultant, Mr. Dino Maselli, to assist in decommissioning its
mill site and disposing of its property. Mr. Maselli has considerable expertise
and experience in the disposition of used equipment. He has assessed the value
of the movable assets at something just less than $40,000. In his opinion, that
figure would have to be discounted to take account of the cost of selling, the
cost of depreciation between now and the time the trial in this matter is
likely to be concluded, and a variety of other factors, in order to obtain a
true resale value. As to the fixed assets, Mr. Maselli concludes that little
value should be ascribed to them unless they are sold as part of the mill site.
They would then only have value to a potential purchaser if the potential
purchaser were looking to purchase a mill site and a salmon hatchery, something
of a remote prospect it would appear.

[
22
] I accept Mr.
Maselli's estimates given his experience and the reasonably detailed basis he
has provided for them. The major fixed assets are not "exigible" in
any real sense. Thus, the plaintiff has available something less than $40,000
in exigible assets. Even that figure has to be discounted for the reasons set
out above in order to realistically ascertain the funds that would be available
to satisfy any potential award of costs.

[
23
] In summary,
the plaintiff has not shown that it has sufficient assets to satisfy the anticipated
costs of this litigation. It is worth noting, however, that the plaintiff is
not devoid of assets; it is not a shell company being manipulated by
individuals for the purpose of avoiding exposure to the costs of unsuccessful
litigation. It has assets which, even on a conservative approach, are capable
of satisfying a portion of the anticipated costs, if the plaintiff's litigation
proves unsuccessful.

[
24
] The third
preliminary issue involves a consideration of whether the defendant has an
arguable case. The short answer to this question is yes. The plaintiff is
seeking a declaration that it has an irrevocable licence to occupy lands owned
by the defendant. The defendant asserts that the plaintiff has occupied the
lands at the defendant's pleasure. There is no written agreement between the
parties purporting to establish or convey an interest in the land. Further, the
defendant argues that it has not been paid for any alleged interest, to the
contrary, it has beneficently supported the plaintiff by, among other things,
providing it with power and other utilities. There is, in my view, an arguable
defence.

CONSIDERATIONS
AFFECTING THE EXERCISE OF THE COURT'S DISCRETION

[
25
] The plaintiff
argues that there are three significant matters all of which militate against
ordering that it post security for costs. Firstly, the plaintiff argues that by
requiring it to post security for costs, it will effectively be prevented from
prosecuting its claim. Secondly, it argues that one reason for the plaintiff's
relative impecuniosity is the conduct of the defendant. Finally, the plaintiff
argues that the defendant has advanced a counterclaim, which will likely be
litigated regardless of whether the plaintiff's claim proceeds. The plaintiff
contends that the issues relevant to the counterclaim to a significant degree
overlap with the issues relevant to the plaintiff's claim. In the result, the
plaintiff argues that it would be unfair to order it to post security for
costs.

[
26
] In order to
successfully resist an order for security for costs on the basis that such an
order would effectively stifle the plaintiff's claim, the plaintiff must show
that it has "insufficient assets and no means of raising money for
security":
Citizens For Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
[1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (B.C.S.C.)
per Romilly J. (See also
Honda
Canada Inc. v. Tonka Motorcycle Sales

(1986),
7 B.C.L.R. (2d) 136
(B.C.S.C.)
).

[
27
] In support of
its contention, the plaintiff has, through the affidavit of Mr. Frame, set out
its financial circumstances. Mr. Frame's affidavit, as amplified by his
cross-examination, tends to support the conclusion that the plaintiff's
financial circumstances are such that it would be difficult to continue with
this law suit, if it were required to post the full amount of security as
claimed by the defendant. Categoric conclusions on this aspect of the
plaintiff's argument are not possible due to the confusing state of the
financial evidence provided through Mr. Frame.

[
28
] Aside from its
own circumstances, however, the plaintiff must demonstrate that it has no means
of raising money for security. I am not satisfied that the plaintiff has
established that it does not have the ability to raise funds for security for
costs. Unlike the plaintiff, Chin-Ho Aqua is not a "not for profit"
society. It is a private company in relation to which Dale Frame is a director
and vice-president, and John Frame is a director and president. It stands to
benefit if the plaintiff is successful in this litigation. There is evidence
that at least some of the plaintiff's legal fees incurred to November 21, 2001,
(the date that Dale Frame was cross-examined) were paid by Chin-Ho Aqua.

[
29
] The defendant
points to a number of authorities, including
3473 Investments Ltd. v. Orr
et al.
,
[1992] B.C.J. No. 1140 (B.C.S.C.)
per Master Joyce,
East
Broadway Residents' Association v. The City of Vancouver et al.
,
2000 BCCA 657 (CanLII)
,
[2000]
B.C.J. No. 2460 (B.C.C.A.)
, and
Granville Constructors Ltd. v. West
Vancouver School District No. 25
,
[1998] B.C.J. No. 1106 (B.C.S.C.)
, in
which courts have required that plaintiffs post security for costs on the basis
that while the plaintiff itself might be incapable of posting security, there
are others who stand to benefit from the litigation related to the plaintiff
that can assist the plaintiff in posting security. In my view, that is
essentially the situation in the case before me. Accordingly, I find that the
plaintiff has not established that it does not have the means of raising the
funds to post security.

[
30
] The plaintiff
next argues that its inability to post security has at least been partially
caused by the defendant's conduct. If that is so, it is a matter, according to
the plaintiff, for the court to consider in determining whether, and if so how
much, security ought to be ordered. (See:
Tour-Mate Technologies
Corporation et al. v. Syntronix Systems Ltd. et al.
,
1993 CanLII 2250 (BC SC)
,
[1993] B.C.J. No.
599 (B.C.S.C.)
).

[
31
] There are two
actions by the defendant that are said to ground this aspect of the plaintiff's
argument: firstly, the defendant refused to continue paying for the plaintiff's
hydro and other utilities in February 1999 and, secondly, the defendant granted
a lease to Gold River Smolt Company Ltd., thus reducing the plaintiff's income
by $3,000 per month in accordance with the terms of the contract noted above.

[
32
] In
Tour-Mate
,

supra
, the actions of the defendant that were said to have caused or
contributed to the plaintiff's impecuniosity were the subject matter of the
outstanding litigation. The issue, broadly stated, in
Tour-Mate

was whether the defendant was entitled, in law, to do what it did. In those
circumstances, the court held that the defendant's conduct was a basis for
reducing the amount of security ordered.

[
33
] The plaintiff
in this case does not suggest, as I understand their position, that the
defendant was in any way bound to continue paying for the plaintiff's hydro and
other utilities. The evidence discloses that the defendant gave the plaintiff
notice in November of 1998 that because it was shutting down its mill it would
no longer be able to provide these services to the plaintiff effective the
middle of February, 1999. The plaintiff accepted that decision without
complaint and has not sought relief in the context of the within litigation in
relation to that act. Further, as I understand it, the plaintiff does not
suggest that the defendant was not entitled to lease its own lands to Gold
River Smolt. Again, were it otherwise, one might expect there to have been a
claim for relief in the context of this litigation. There is none.

[
34
] Unlike the
situation in
Tour-Mate
,
supra
, the defendant has not done
anything that it was not entitled to do. It is obvious that the defendant's
actions have exacerbated the plaintiff's financial circumstances but the
actions were not, on the evidence, taken for the purpose of hindering the
plaintiff's ability to prosecute this claim, nor were the actions themselves
actionable at the instance of the plaintiff. In these circumstances, they are
not, in my view, a basis upon which to reduce or decline an order for security
for costs.

[
35
] The plaintiff
argues that both sides are seeking relief in this litigation. Further, the
plaintiff suggests that the primary relief being sought by the parties are
mirror images of each other. The plaintiff seeks a declaration together with
ancillary relief; the defendant seeks a declaration together with ancillary
relief. The plaintiff says that it commenced this action because of its need,
following the receipt of the eviction notice, to secure an interim injunction
to preserve the status quo pending resolution of the outstanding issues. But
for that circumstance, the plaintiff argues, this action might just as well
have been commenced by the defendant, in which case the plaintiff would not
have been obliged to post security for costs.

[
36
] The defendant
argues that the plaintiff commenced the action and, regardless of what may or
may not have happened in other circumstances, the court must deal with the
circumstances as they now are. Further, the defendant says that the proposed
costs, which support the claim for security, are exclusive of the costs of the
counterclaim. Finally, the defendant argues that, in effect, but for the plaintiff's
claim, there would be no counterclaim.

[
37
] In my view, it
does not necessarily follow that if the plaintiff's claim were stayed or
withdrawn, the matter would be resolved. The defendant's may well still seek
the declaratory and injunctive relief they have claimed in their counterclaim.
Indeed, it is likely they would seek such relief, particularly if the plaintiff
simply remained on the property in dispute. Nor does it follow, as the
plaintiff argues, that if it were defending these proceedings, it would not be
liable to post security. If the roles were reversed, the plaintiff would, in
all likelihood, do what the defendant has done, namely, counterclaim. If that
were to occur, the plaintiff may be required to post security for costs
relating to its counterclaim.

[
38
] It may be that
the bill of costs is exclusive of costs associated with the counterclaim. The
trial will, however, resolve the issues raised in the counterclaim. The
evidence necessary to defeat the plaintiff's claim will likely be substantially
the same as the evidence required to advance the defendant's counterclaim. On
that basis, part of the costs of this litigation are properly attributable to
the counterclaim. I note that the same would be so if the roles were reversed.

[
39
] In summary, I
am satisfied that it is proper to reduce the amount of security claimed to
account for the cost of litigating the counterclaim. On the material before me,
it is impossible to do that with precision. I will, in my discretion, fix the
amount required to be posted as security at $30,000. I am not satisfied that
the plaintiff will be unable to post security in this amount, such that its
claim would be stifled.

[
40
] The plaintiff
has requested that if security for costs is ordered that it be permitted to
post it at staged intervals. The trial in this matter is set for June 2003. I
order that the plaintiff provide security for costs as follows:

(a) in the amount
of $10,000 on or before May 1, 2002;

(b) in the further
amount of $10,000 on or before October 1, 2002; and

(c) in the further
amount of $10,000 on or before February 1, 2003.

In the event the
plaintiff has failed to post security on or before the dates ordered, the
proceeding against the defendant shall be stayed and the defendant will,
thereafter, be at liberty to apply for a dismissal of the action.

[
41
] The costs of
this application will be in the cause.

"G.M. Barrow, J."

The Honourable Mr. Justice G.M. Barrow
